The Conservative Party is one of the two major political forces in British history, emerging as a modern organized party during the nineteenth century. It traditionally represents property owners, the established church, and social stability, opposing radical reform. The party has shaped British governance for nearly two centuries and remains central to UK politics, alternating power with its rival, the Liberal Party. The Conservative Party traces its ideological roots to the Tory faction of the seventeenth century, which supported royal authority during the English Civil War. It formally crystallized as a modern party under Benjamin Disraeli in the 1870s, when he repositioned it as an imperialist force appealing to working-class voters. The party was dominated by nineteenth-century leaders like Robert Peel, who championed gradual reform while resisting revolutionary change. The Conservatives won support from both the landed aristocracy and urban middle classes by embracing imperial expansion and opposing radical socialism. They reached their peak under Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s, when her government pursued radical free-market economics and weakened trade unions. The party stands in perpetual tension with the Liberal Party and later the Labour Party as the right-wing pole of British two-party politics. Core Conservative ideology emphasizes tradition, property rights, national sovereignty, and a hierarchical social order tempered by noblesse oblige and constitutional governance. Major policy platforms include opposition to the welfare state, though accepting its basic existence, skepticism of European integration, and emphasis on law and order. The Conservatives alternated power with the Liberals and later Labour throughout the twentieth century, dominating the nineteen twenties and thirties, the nineteen fifties and sixties, and the nineteen eighties and nineties.
